Bootstrapped business: Precision Aesthetics Lab

[ops][assistant] To get us started, could you describe in plain language what "Precision Aesthetics Lab" does or will do—what you sell or deliver, and how you expect to get paid for it (if it's easier, you can start with something simple like "fitness gym", "law firm", "restaurant", etc.)?
[user] Precision Aesthetics Lab provides advanced non-surgical aesthetic treatments with a focus on high-ticket procedures delivered in a clinical studio setting. We perform all treatments in person at our Dallas studio, and clients primarily book and pay through online scheduling triggered by our paid advertising.

[ops][assistant] Here’s how I’m understanding Precision Aesthetics Lab:

This is an in-person aesthetics clinic that delivers advanced, non-surgical cosmetic treatments (for example things like injectables, skin resurfacing, or similar high-ticket procedures) performed in a clinical studio setting. Revenue comes from clients booking individual treatment appointments and paying per visit or per treatment package, with most bookings initiated through your online scheduling system that’s driven by paid advertising. Operationally, it functions as a clinic offering discrete treatment sessions rather than a membership/subscription model, so a typical “unit” for planning is one in-person treatment appointment, and we’ll treat that on a weekly cadence (how many appointments you can handle in a typical week).

Is this an accurate high-level description of how the business works?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Based on the start date you provided, I'm treating this as operating for planning context. If that's off, tell me and I'll adjust.

Next, do you primarily serve individual consumers, other businesses (for example as a white-label provider for medspas/clinics), or a mix of both?
[user] Primarily individual consumers.

[ops][assistant] Got it, primarily individual consumers.

For planning, let’s focus on your main “treatment appointment” unit. In a fully booked, typical week at your Dallas studio, about how many treatment appointments can you realistically handle (total, across all clients and treatment types)?
[user] We can handle up to 55 treatment sessions per week at full capacity.

[ops][assistant] Great, 55 treatment sessions per week at full capacity.

For Year 1, you typically won’t be fully booked all the time. A practical assumption for many clinics at your stage is using around 70–80% of that capacity on average. Does using about 75% of your weekly capacity (so roughly three-quarters of those 55 slots filled on average) feel about right for Year 1?
[user] Actually, we plan to use about 88% utilization in Year 1, so closer to 48 or 49 sessions per week on average, not just 75%.

[ops][assistant] Perfect, we’ll plan on about 88% utilization in Year 1, so roughly 48–49 treatment sessions per week on average out of your 55-slot capacity.

Next, let’s nail down pricing for a typical treatment appointment: on average, how much do you expect to collect per in-person treatment session (blending across the high-ticket procedures you offer)?
[user] The average price per treatment session is $875.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, we’ll use an average of $875 per treatment session.

Since all treatments are performed in person at your Dallas studio and booked online, I’ll assume the main way clients receive the service is by coming into the clinic for an in-person appointment at your location. Is that accurate?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, that’s clear.

Because treatments are only delivered in person at your Dallas studio and bookings are primarily online, I’ll assume your sales model is “hybrid” — marketing and scheduling happen online, but fulfillment is in-person at the clinic. Does “hybrid” as the main sales channel description fit how you operate?
[user] Yes, that's right. Clients primarily book through paid ads and online scheduling.

[ops][assistant] Given your Dallas studio location and in-person treatment model, I’ll assume your service area is primarily local—patients coming from Dallas and nearby communities in Dallas County (for example, central Dallas, Uptown, and surrounding neighborhoods). Does describing your geographic reach as “local: Dallas and nearby areas in Dallas County, Texas” fit how you operate?
[user] Our geographic reach is the Dallas metro area, and we do have some clients traveling from surrounding regions, not just within Dallas County.

[ops][assistant] Got it, so your reach is broader than just the city/county and really functions at a Dallas–Fort Worth metro level, with some clients coming in from neighboring regions.

For our notes, I’d like to capture that as “regional” coverage centered on the DFW metro. Does this wording work for you: “Dallas–Fort Worth metro area plus nearby North Texas communities such as Plano, Frisco, Arlington, and Irving”?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] Thanks, that matches what I’ll note for your service area.

Based on how these clinics typically run, I’ll assume fulfillment works like this: treatments are performed personally by you and/or a small clinical team in the Dallas studio, patients book specific time slots online, and you deliver the procedures during those scheduled appointments with a typical lead time of a few days to a couple of weeks depending on demand. The main thing that limits how many appointments you can do is your and your team’s available clinical time (treatment room hours and provider hours), not software or lack of demand once marketing is working. That is how fulfillment typically works for this kind of business – does this look right?
[user] Yes, that's correct.

[ops][assistant] One quick structural detail before we wrap the ops side: what’s the legal structure you’re using for Precision Aesthetics Lab (for example Sole proprietor, LLC, S-corp, C-corp, Partnership, LLP)?
[user] We are operating as an LLC.

[ops][assistant] Proposed competitive advantage: Your primary competitive advantage is a tightly controlled, high-yield appointment model that deliberately trades volume for revenue-per-hour by focusing on fewer, longer, and more complex treatment sessions at a premium price point, instead of stacking short, low-ticket visits. This is enabled operationally by designing the menu, scheduling rules, and marketing funnel specifically around high-value procedures (rather than “any aesthetic service”), which makes your limited clinical time produce significantly more revenue per provider hour and allows more focus and consistency in each visit. Competitors struggle to copy this because it requires reconfiguring their entire business logic—pricing, promotion, room utilization, and provider incentives—away from familiar high-churn models, which creates real financial and cultural friction for them.

Does this accurately reflect what truly sets the business apart?
[user] Yes, that description perfectly captures our competitive advantage and how we operate Precision Aesthetics Lab. We focus on maximizing revenue per provider hour with fewer, high-value treatments rather than volume-based low-ticket sessions.

[ops][assistant] Looking ahead, what is one concrete goal you want to hit in about the next 12 months (for example: a target number of weekly units/orders, a customer count, or a rough monthly revenue level)?
[user] Our goal within the next 12 months is to reach about 70 treatment sessions per week.

[market][assistant] Great, let's move on to Target Market.

Given your high-ticket, in-person aesthetic treatments, do you want to focus primarily on women, primarily on men, or serve all genders roughly equally?
[user] Mostly female but open to all.

[market][assistant] Got it — we’ll treat your target as primarily female while still being open to all genders.

Next, what age range are you mainly designing Precision Aesthetics Lab for (for example, 25–45, 30–60, etc.)?
[user] We're targeting adults aged 30 to 65 primarily, with a focus on that age group for the treatments.

[market][assistant] Great, we’ll center your primary target on adults ages 30 to 65, while still being open to clients outside that band.

Next, thinking about income: given your high-ticket average of $875 per session, what household income range are you mainly targeting (for example, “upper-middle income and above,” or something like “$100k–$250k+ per year”) so that pricing feels realistic for your ideal clients?
[user] We're targeting households with an income of $60,000 and above to match the pricing of our advanced treatments.

[market][assistant] Thanks, we’ll target households with income of about $60,000 and above, which is workable for your pricing, though in practice many of your best, most frequent clients may skew higher within that band.

Next, how much does formal education level matter for your ideal clients—are you essentially open to all education levels, or do you mainly expect/aim for clients with college degrees and above?
[user] We're open to mixed education levels among our clients, so we don't restrict our target based on formal education.

[market][assistant] Education noted as open/mixed with no specific requirement.

Given your high-ticket, elective aesthetic nature and Dallas metro focus, it *could* help targeting to know more about personal/household context (for example, dual-income households, certain job types, or housing situations), but it’s optional.

Which, if any, of these do you want to define more clearly for your target market: household structure, employment, housing economics, any combination of those, or would you prefer to skip all three and keep it simple?
[user] We prefer to keep it simple and skip detailed definitions for household structure and housing economics, but we do consider a mix of professionals and service workers in terms of employment sectors.

[market][assistant] Precision Aesthetics Lab should be positioned as a regional, premium advanced aesthetics clinic offering high-ticket, non-surgical treatments sold per in-person treatment appointment rather than via memberships or subscriptions, with each appointment priced around $875. Operating from a Dallas-based clinical studio and drawing from the broader DFW metro, the brand should emphasize expertise, safety, and outcome-focused care for primarily female adults aged 30 to 65 with mid-to-upper income households, while remaining welcoming to all genders and education levels. Because the core constraint is clinical labor and treatment-room time rather than software or physical reach, messaging should focus on the value and sophistication of each high-yield session, appealing to appearance-conscious professionals and service workers who can afford discretionary, premium treatments and are willing to travel within the region for quality.

For acquisition, Google Search should be a core channel because high-intent prospects often begin with procedure-specific or symptom-specific queries when actively looking for advanced, higher-priced aesthetic solutions in their area. Google Maps/Business Profile should support this by capturing local and regional searchers comparing nearby clinics and validating their choice through proximity, reviews, and clinical imagery. Instagram should be used to showcase before-and-after results, practitioner expertise, and the elevated studio environment, which aligns well with visually driven, appearance-focused clients in the 30–65 age band. Meta (Facebook/Instagram) paid ads should continue as a primary driver of online bookings, using precise geographic and demographic filters to reach higher-income adults across the DFW metro who are amenable to premium cash-pay procedures. Referral partnerships with complementary local providers (such as salons, wellness studios, or fitness concepts) should round out acquisition by tapping into existing trust networks of clients predisposed to invest in their appearance. This narrative defines the strategic marketing architecture and will be expanded into a detailed execution-level marketing plan in the full written business plan.

Does this look right before we move on to Human Resources?
[user] Yes, that captures our target market and marketing approach accurately. We are ready to move on to Human Resources.

[people][assistant] Great, let's move on to Human Resources.

For Precision Aesthetics Lab at this operating stage, businesses often highlight just a few pivotal roles (leadership, clinical/licensed providers, operations, and key client-facing people), as targeted additions to an already running model rather than a full rebuild.

Let’s start with you or the primary leader. For the first person, please share in one go:
- Full name  
- Current title/role in the business  
- Years of relevant experience in aesthetics/healthcare/related fields (numeric is fine, e.g., 7)  
- Relevant education and professional credentials (degrees, licenses, certifications—if any are unknown or not applicable, you can say “none”)
[user] The founder is a licensed nurse practitioner with 6 years of experience in aesthetics.

[people][assistant] Thanks, that helps. I’d like to capture this person properly by name and credentials.

For this founder/lead provider, could you share in one combined reply:
- Full name  
- Their exact current title in the business (for example, “Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner” or whatever you use)  
- Years of relevant experience (can I confirm it’s 6 years total in aesthetics/healthcare combined, or 6 specifically in aesthetics?)  
- Their key education and credentials (for example: nursing degree(s), NP credentials, board certifications, aesthetic certifications, etc.—“none” is fine if something doesn’t apply)  

Once we have this person, I’ll ask if you’d like to add another.
[user] The founder's name is Taylor Morgan. Their exact current title is "Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner." They have 6 years of experience specifically in aesthetics. Their key credentials include a Master of Science in Nursing, Nurse Practitioner license, and certification in advanced aesthetic procedures.

[people][assistant] Got it, thank you for that detail on Taylor Morgan.

Would you like to add another person who is important to how Precision Aesthetics Lab actually runs today (for example another provider, operations/clinic manager, marketing lead, medical director, or key client-facing staff)? If yes, please share in one reply:
- Full name  
- Current title/role in the business  
- Years of relevant experience (numeric)  
- Relevant education and credentials (degrees, licenses, certifications, or “none” if not applicable)
[user] No, there are no additional staff at launch. Taylor Morgan is the sole key person running Precision Aesthetics Lab at this time.

[people][assistant] Review this draft (key people narrative + suggested year-1 roles with wages and timing) and tell me any changes.

As Founder & Lead Aesthetic Nurse Practitioner, Taylor Morgan brings a Master of Science in Nursing, a Nurse Practitioner license, certification in advanced aesthetic procedures, and 6 years of focused aesthetics experience to Precision Aesthetics Lab, enabling safe delivery of complex, high-ticket treatments and evidence-based clinical decision-making. Taylor personally leads treatment planning, procedure execution, and clinical protocols, while also shaping the service menu, pricing, and booking cadence to align with a high-yield appointment model. This blend of hands-on clinical skill and practical business oversight gives Precision Aesthetics Lab the execution capability to consistently fill and optimize limited treatment-room time, maintain strong patient outcomes, and uphold regulatory and safety standards as the clinic scales. Estimated annual wage: $129,440/year.

Suggested year-1 roles and estimated annual wages:
- Clinic Coordinator / Patient Care Concierge: $39,630/year (in ~6 months) - Needed to manage front-desk operations, scheduling, patient intake, and follow-up so clinical time can be devoted primarily to delivering high-value treatments as weekly sessions approach higher utilization.
- Part-Time Marketing & Patient Acquisition Specialist: $46,760/year (in ~6 months) - Needed to run and optimize paid ads, online booking funnels, and basic content so the clinic can reliably fill premium appointment slots without pulling Taylor away from treatment time.
- Additional Aesthetic Nurse or Mid-Level Provider (Part-Time to Full-Time): $129,440/year (in ~12 months) - Needed to add clinical capacity and reduce bottlenecks on provider time as demand grows toward and beyond 70 treatments per week, enabling more throughput without compromising visit quality.

Does this look right before we move on to Financials?
[user] Yes, that looks right.

[financials][assistant] Great, let's move on to Financials.

Year 1 revenue:

| Line of Business | Product / Unit | Capacity | Load / Utilization | Price | Periods / Year | Year-1 Revenue |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Primary line of business | treatment appointment | 55 treatment appointment/week | 88% | $875 | 52 | $2,202,200 |
| **Primary line of business total** |  |  |  |  |  | **$2,202,200** |
| **Company Total** |  |  |  |  |  | **$2,202,200** |

This planning baseline assumes you run at about 88% utilization of 55 sessions per week, at an average price of $875, across 52 operating periods, which produces about $2,202,200 in Year-1 revenue. We will use this as the baseline for the rest of financial planning.
[user] Yes, that's right.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll use $2,202,200 as the Year-1 revenue baseline for the financial plan.

Based on the people plan already defined, a reasonable Year-1 payroll baseline is about $172,635 across 4 roles in the plan.

This payroll estimate reflects the existing team plus any incremental additions from the staffing plan; it is not replacing the team already in place. That includes 1 current team role and 3 additional planned roles.

Does that broadly match your Year-1 payroll expectation, or should we adjust it because your actual payroll setup is materially different?
[user] The Year-1 payroll expectation is only for the owner; there are no additional hires initially, so please use just the owner payroll amount of $120,000 for Year 1.

[financials][assistant] Got it — we’ll set Year-1 payroll to just the owner at $120,000 and remove the additional hires from the Year-1 payroll baseline.

A reasonable Year-1 marketing baseline is about 23% of revenue, which puts your projected Year-1 marketing spend around $506,506.

Does that broadly match what it will take to attract and convert customers in Year 1, or should we adjust it because your marketing spend will be materially different?
[user] That marketing spend estimate is higher than we plan to spend. We are aiming for a lower marketing budget than 23% of revenue in Year 1 to manage costs carefully.

[financials][assistant] Got it—roughly what percent of revenue (or dollar amount) do you want to use for your Year-1 marketing budget instead of 23%?

What do you pay each month for the space you use to run the business, like an office, storefront, clinic, kitchen, warehouse, or similar dedicated space?
[user] For Year 1, we plan to allocate a marketing budget lower than the 23% baseline, around 10% of revenue, which would be approximately $220,000. For the space rent, we pay $9,500 per month for the clinic space.

[financials][assistant] Perfect, I’ll set your Year 1 marketing budget to about 10% of revenue (around $220,000) and record your clinic rent at $9,500 per month.

Looking ahead, do you expect paid dedicated business space to stay part of how this business operates?
[user] Yes, that's right. We plan to maintain paid dedicated business space as an ongoing part of our operational model.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll record that you expect to keep paying for dedicated business space going forward.

As of last month, how much did you pay yourself from the business in wages, draws, or other owner compensation? A dollar amount is fine.
[user] I paid myself $10,000 last month, consistent with the annual owner compensation of $120,000.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record your owner compensation as $120,000 per year based on the $10,000 per month you’re paying yourself.

As of last month, about how much did you spend on other regular business bills besides payroll, marketing, and rent, like utilities, software, insurance, accounting, phone, internet, and general overhead?
[user] Other regular monthly business expenses are about $4,000 per month. This includes utilities, software, insurance, accounting, phone, internet, and general overhead.

[financials][assistant] Got it—I'll plug in $4,000 per month for other operating expenses.

As of last month, how many people were on payroll for the business, not counting outside contractors? A whole number is fine.
[user] There was only 1 person on payroll last month, which is myself as the owner.

[financials][assistant] Thanks—I'll record 1 current employee on payroll (you as the owner).

As of last month, did you make any larger one-time purchases for the business, like equipment, devices, furniture, build-out, or vehicles? If yes, what was the rough total?
[user] Yes, we made larger one-time purchases totaling around $60,000 recently for equipment and build-out.

[financials][assistant] Got it—I'll record about $60,000 as your recent one-time equipment/build-out spending.

As of last month, what is your best rough estimate of the total value of the main equipment, devices, furniture, and fixtures already in the business?
[user] The total value of the main equipment, devices, furniture, and fixtures in the business is approximately $180,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it, I’ll record your current equipment, furniture, and fixtures at about $180,000.

Now let's capture any leased or rented equipment or space beyond your main rent. What monthly amount should we use for any leased equipment, vehicles, servers, or additional space you do not own? If there is none, use 0.
[user] We use $2,500 per month for leased equipment or additional leased space beyond our main rent.

[financials][assistant] Great, I’ll record $2,500 per month for leased equipment or additional leased space beyond your main rent.

As of last month, what is your best rough estimate of the total money or value put into the business so far by you or any investors?
[user] The total money or value put into the business so far by me and any investors is $50,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $50,000 as the total equity invested into the business so far.

As of last month, what was the total amount the business still owed on loans, lines of credit, or business credit cards?
[user] The business still owes a total of $120,000 on loans, lines of credit, or business credit cards as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $120,000 as the total debt the business still owes as of last month.

As of last month, besides regular rent and credit card minimums already baked into other expenses, what other loan or debt payments did the business make each month?
[user] The business made other monthly debt payments of $1,500 as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record $1,500 per month as your other monthly debt payments.

Of your debt payments, what is your best estimate of the annual interest cost, meaning the finance charge rather than principal paydown?
[user] The annual interest cost on the debt payments is about $9,000.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record your annual interest cost as about $9,000.

What is your best estimate of the annual principal you expect to repay on the business debt, separate from interest?
[user] The annual principal payment on the business debt is about $18,000.

[financials][assistant] Thanks — I’ll record your annual principal repayment as about $18,000.

As of last month, about how much cash did the business have on hand in its bank accounts and any cash on site?
[user] The business had about $15,000 in cash on hand as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record cash on hand as about $15,000.

As of last month, about how much money did customers still owe you for completed work, like unpaid invoices or payment plans?
[user] Customers still owed about $2,000 for completed work as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record about $2,000 as your accounts receivable balance.

As of last month, about how much did the business still owe in regular operating bills, like unpaid supplier invoices, utilities, or business credit card balances related to operations?
[user] The business still owed about $12,000 in regular operating bills as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Got it — I’ll record about $12,000 as your accounts payable balance.

As of last month, about how much inventory did you have on hand, like products or supplies kept in stock to use or sell?
[user] The business had about $15,000 worth of inventory on hand as of last month.

[financials][assistant] Thanks, I’ll record your inventory balance as about $15,000 as of last month.

One last financial planning question before I wrap this section up: when this business starts building extra cash, what would you want to do with it?

- Reinvest: Use extra cash to fund growth, capacity, or expansion when the economics support it.
- Preserve cash: Keep a thicker cash cushion and stay more conservative about putting excess cash back to work.
- Shareholder return: Treat excess cash as something that can be taken out of the business rather than just left to build up.
- Balanced: Keep a healthy cushion while still reinvesting selectively when it makes sense.

You can answer in plain language and I'll map it to the closest approach.
[user] I plan to reinvest any extra cash back into the business to fund hiring, expansion, and growth opportunities when the economics support it.

[done][assistant] Got it—I'll mark your cash strategy as focused on reinvesting excess cash back into the business for growth.

Thanks. I have everything I need for financials, and the intake is complete.
